description: AP Calculus AB prep - limits, derivatives, integrals
title: AP Calculus AB (12th)

questions.question: Find lim (x -> 2) (x^2 - 4) / (x - 2).
questions.explanation: Factor: (x^2 - 4) = (x - 2)(x + 2). Cancel (x - 2) to get x + 2. Then lim (x -> 2) (x + 2) = 4.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: factor first, cancel the troublemaker, then plug in - dino demolition!

questions.question: Find lim (x -> 0) sin(x) / x.
questions.explanation: This is the fundamental trigonometric limit. On the unit circle, cos(x) < sin(x)/x < 1 for small nonzero x, and both bounds approach 1, so by the Squeeze Theorem lim (x -> 0) sin(x)/x = 1.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: sine over x near zero always lands at one - memorize it like a dino roar!

questions.question: Find lim (x -> 3) (2x + 1).
questions.explanation: Direct substitution: 2(3) + 1 = 7.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: if plugging in works, just plug in - no drama!

questions.question: Find lim (x -> 1) (x^3 - 1) / (x - 1).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: difference of cubes - (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2) - then cancel and chill!

questions.question: Find lim (x -> infinity) (3x^2 + 2x) / (5x^2 - x).
questions.explanation: Divide top and bottom by x^2: (3 + 2/x) / (5 - 1/x). As x -> infinity, terms with 1/x go to 0, leaving 3/5.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: top degree equals bottom degree - the limit is the ratio of leading coefficients!

questions.question: Find lim (x -> infinity) (x^3 + 1) / (2x^2 - 5).
questions.explanation: Top degree (3) is greater than bottom degree (2), and the ratio is positive, so the limit is infinity.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: top degree wins the race - limit blows up to infinity!

questions.question: Find lim (x -> -infinity) (4x + 7) / (2x^2 + 3).
questions.explanation: Bottom degree (2) is greater than top degree (1), so the limit is 0.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: bottom degree bigger - the limit sinks to zero like a tired dino!

questions.question: Find lim (x -> 0+) 1 / x.
questions.explanation: Approaching 0 from the right, 1/x grows without bound in the positive direction: infinity.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: tiny positive denominator, big positive result - infinity party!

questions.question: Find the left-hand limit of 1 / x as x approaches 0.
questions.explanation: Approaching 0 from the left, 1/x grows without bound in the negative direction: -infinity.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: from the left side the sign flips - negative infinity dive!

questions.question: Find lim (x -> 0) |x| / x.
questions.explanation: Right-hand limit is 1, left-hand limit is -1. Since they disagree, the two-sided limit does not exist.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: left says -1, right says 1 - when the sides fight, the limit does not exist!

questions.question: Find lim (x -> 4) sqrt(x + 5).
questions.explanation: Direct substitution: sqrt(4 + 5) = sqrt(9) = 3.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: roots are continuous where defined - just plug in!

questions.question: Find lim (x -> 0) (1 - cos(x)) / x.
questions.explanation: Multiply top and bottom by (1 + cos(x)): (1 - cos^2(x)) / (x(1 + cos(x))) = sin^2(x) / (x(1 + cos(x))). Then (sin(x)/x) * (sin(x)/(1 + cos(x))) -> 1 * 0 = 0.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: one minus cosine over x always melts to zero - trust the trick!

questions.question: Find lim (x -> 5) (x^2 - 25) / (x^2 - 3x - 10).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: factor both, cancel the twin, then substitute - dino double-takedown!

questions.question: Find lim (x -> 2) (sqrt(x + 2) - 2) / (x - 2).
questions.explanation: Multiply by the conjugate (sqrt(x+2) + 2): ((x + 2) - 4) / ((x - 2)(sqrt(x+2) + 2)) = 1 / (sqrt(x+2) + 2). At x = 2: 1/4.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: root on top? Multiply by the conjugate - the classic dino ambush!

questions.question: Find lim (x -> infinity) (1 + 3/x)^x.
questions.explanation: This matches the form lim (x -> infinity) (1 + a/x)^x = e^a with a = 3, so the limit is e^3.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: one plus a-over-x to the x - that is e to the a, every time!

questions.question: If lim (x -> c) f(x) = 4 and lim (x -> c) g(x) = -2, find lim (x -> c) [f(x) * g(x)].
questions.explanation: Limit of a product is the product of the limits: 4 * (-2) = -8.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: limits play nice with arithmetic - multiply the answers!

questions.question: Find lim (x -> 1) (x^2 + 3x - 4) / (x^2 - 1).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: spot the (x - 1) twins, cancel them, then plug in!

questions.question: Find lim (x -> 0) (e^x - 1) / x.
questions.explanation: This is a standard limit equal to 1 - it is the definition of the derivative of e^x at x = 0.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: e-to-the-x minus one over x - the answer is one, done!

questions.question: Find lim (x -> infinity) ln(x) / x.
questions.explanation: Logarithms grow slower than any power of x, so ln(x)/x -> 0 as x -> infinity.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: logs are slowpokes - any power of x outruns them to zero!

questions.question: Find lim (x -> 3-) (x + 1) / (x - 3).
questions.explanation: Numerator approaches 4 (positive), denominator approaches 0 from the negative side, so the quotient goes to -infinity.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: positive over tiny-negative - negative infinity nosedive!

questions.question: Determine whether f(x) = (x^2 - 9) / (x - 3) is continuous at x = 3.
questions.correctAnswer: No, it has a removable discontinuity
distractors: No, it has a jump discontinuity
No, it has an infinite discontinuity
questions.explanation: f(3) is undefined (0/0 form), but the limit as x -> 3 exists and equals 6. A function must be defined at the point to be continuous, so this is a removable discontinuity.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: hole in the graph? Removable - the dino can patch it with one point!

questions.question: Identify which condition must hold for f to be continuous at x = c.
questions.correctAnswer: f(c) is defined, lim (x -> c) f(x) exists, and they are equal
questions.explanation: Continuity at c requires all three: the function value exists, the limit exists, and the limit equals the function value.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: defined, limit exists, and they match - the continuity triple-check!

questions.question: Identify the type of discontinuity of f(x) = 1 / (x - 2) at x = 2.
questions.explanation: As x approaches 2, f(x) goes to infinity (or -infinity), so the function has a vertical asymptote - an infinite discontinuity.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: denominator zero with no cancel - vertical asymptote, infinite blast-off!

questions.question: Find the value of k that makes f continuous at x = 2, where f(x) = x^2 + 1 for x < 2 and f(x) = kx + 3 for x >= 2.
questions.explanation: Left limit: 2^2 + 1 = 5. Right value: k(2) + 3 = 2k + 3. Set equal: 2k + 3 = 5, so k = 1.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: make the two sides shake hands at the boundary - set them equal!

questions.question: Determine whether f(x) = |x| is continuous at x = 0.
questions.explanation: f(0) = 0 and lim (x -> 0) |x| = 0, so all three continuity conditions hold even though the function is not differentiable there.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: absolute value has a corner but no break - continuous, just pointy!

questions.question: Determine the interval on which f(x) = sqrt(x - 1) is continuous.
questions.explanation: The square root requires x - 1 >= 0, so x >= 1. The function is continuous on its entire domain [1, infinity).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: continuous wherever it lives - check the domain first!

questions.question: If f is continuous on [a, b] and f(a) < 0 < f(b), what does the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantee?
questions.correctAnswer: There is a c in (a, b) with f(c) = 0
distractors: f has a maximum on [a, b]
questions.explanation: The IVT says a continuous function takes on every value between f(a) and f(b), so it must cross zero somewhere in (a, b).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: continuous from negative to positive - it MUST cross zero somewhere in between!

questions.question: Identify where the greatest integer function f(x) = floor(x) is discontinuous:
questions.explanation: floor(x) jumps at every integer (e.g., lim (x -> 2-) = 1 but f(2) = 2), so it has jump discontinuities at all integers.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: floor function stomps up stairs - a jump at every integer step!

questions.question: Using the definition of derivative, f'(x) = lim (h -> 0) [f(x + h) - f(x)] / h. If f(x) = x^2, find f'(3).
questions.explanation: f'(x) = 2x by the power rule, so f'(3) = 6. Via definition: lim (h -> 0) [(3+h)^2 - 9]/h = lim (h -> 0) (6h + h^2)/h = 6.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: power rule - bring the power down, subtract one from the exponent!

questions.question: If f(x) = x^5, find f'(x).
questions.explanation: Power rule: d/dx [x^n] = n*x^(n-1), so f'(x) = 5x^4.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: five comes down, exponent drops to four - power rule stomp!

questions.question: If f(x) = 7x^3 - 4x^2 + 2x - 9, find f'(x).
questions.explanation: Differentiate term by term: 21x^2 - 8x + 2 - 0 = 21x^2 - 8x + 2.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: attack each term one at a time - constants vanish into dino dust!

questions.question: If f(x) = sqrt(x), find f'(x).
questions.explanation: Write sqrt(x) = x^(1/2). Power rule: (1/2)x^(-1/2) = 1/(2*sqrt(x)).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: root means half-power - bring down one-half and watch the exponent go negative!

questions.question: If f(x) = 1 / x^2, find f'(x).
questions.explanation: Write 1/x^2 = x^(-2). Power rule: -2x^(-3) = -2/x^3.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: flip it to a negative exponent first, then power rule does the rest!

questions.question: If f(x) = e^x, find f'(x).
questions.explanation: The derivative of e^x is itself: d/dx [e^x] = e^x.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: e-to-the-x is the immortal function - its derivative never changes!

questions.question: If f(x) = ln(x), find f'(x).
questions.explanation: d/dx [ln(x)] = 1/x for x > 0. Reason: ln is the inverse of e^x, and differentiating the inverse gives 1 divided by e^(ln(x)), which is 1/x.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: derivative of ln is one-over-x - short, sweet, unforgettable!

questions.question: If f(x) = sin(x), find f'(x).
questions.explanation: d/dx [sin(x)] = cos(x).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: sine becomes cosine - the trig derivative dance step one!

questions.question: If f(x) = cos(x), find f'(x).
questions.explanation: d/dx [cos(x)] = -sin(x). Watch the negative sign.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: cosine becomes NEGATIVE sine - that minus sign is the trap!

questions.question: If f(x) = tan(x), find f'(x).
questions.explanation: Write tan(x) = sin(x)/cos(x) and apply the quotient rule: (cos^2(x) + sin^2(x)) / cos^2(x) = 1 / cos^2(x) = sec^2(x).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: tan becomes sec-squared - remember the sassy secant!

questions.question: Find the slope of the tangent line to f(x) = x^3 - 2x at x = 2.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: derivative at a point IS the tangent slope - evaluate and go!

questions.question: If f(x) = 4, find f'(x).
questions.explanation: The derivative of any constant is 0.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: flat line, zero slope - constants always differentiate to zero!

questions.question: If f(x) = 3e^x + 2ln(x), find f'(x).
questions.explanation: Differentiate term by term: 3e^x + 2*(1/x) = 3e^x + 2/x.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: e^x stays, ln becomes one-over - term by term, no fear!

questions.question: Find d/dx [x^2 * sin(x)] using the product rule.
questions.explanation: Product rule: (2x)(sin x) + (x^2)(cos x) = 2x*sin(x) + x^2*cos(x).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: first times derivative of second PLUS second times derivative of first - product rule chant!

questions.question: Find d/dx [(x^2 + 1) / (x - 3)] using the quotient rule.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: low d-high minus high d-low, over low-low - quotient rule rhyme!

questions.question: If f(x) = (3x + 1)^4, find f'(x) using the chain rule.
questions.explanation: Chain rule: 4(3x+1)^3 * 3 = 12(3x+1)^3. Do not forget to multiply by the derivative of the inside.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: chain rule - derivative of outside times derivative of inside, never skip the inside!

questions.question: If f(x) = sin(2x), find f'(x).
questions.explanation: Chain rule: cos(2x) * 2 = 2cos(2x).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: the 2 inside must come out - chain rule multiplies by the inner derivative!

questions.question: If f(x) = e^(x^2), find f'(x).
questions.explanation: Chain rule: e^(x^2) * 2x = 2x*e^(x^2).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: e keeps its exponent, then multiply by the exponent's derivative!

questions.question: If f(x) = ln(x^2 + 1), find f'(x).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: ln becomes one-over-inside, then chain on the inside!

questions.question: If f(x) = sqrt(4x^3 + 2), find f'(x).
questions.explanation: Write as (4x^3 + 2)^(1/2). Chain rule: (1/2)(4x^3 + 2)^(-1/2) * 12x^2 = 6x^2 / sqrt(4x^3 + 2). The 1/2 and the 12 multiply to 6 - do not divide by 2 a second time.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: root chain rule - half comes down, inside derivative multiplies, then simplify!

questions.question: Find d/dx [x * e^(3x)].
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: product rule meets chain rule - handle the e^(3x) with a chain inside the product!

questions.question: If y = x^3 + 2x, find dy/dx at the point where x = 1.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: differentiate, then plug in the point - easy dino points!

questions.question: If f(x) = cos^2(x), find f'(x).
questions.explanation: Write as (cos x)^2. Chain rule: 2cos(x) * (-sin(x)) = -2cos(x)sin(x).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: power outside, trig inside - chain them like dino links!

questions.question: Find d/dx [arctan(x)].
questions.explanation: Let y = arctan(x), so x = tan(y). Differentiate implicitly: 1 = sec^2(y) * dy/dx. Since sec^2(y) = 1 + tan^2(y) = 1 + x^2, dy/dx = 1 / (1 + x^2).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: arctan derivative is one over one-plus-x-squared - memorize this gem!

questions.question: Use implicit differentiation: if x^2 + y^2 = 25, find dy/dx.
questions.explanation: Differentiate: 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0. Solve: dy/dx = -x/y.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: y gets a dy/dx buddy every time you differentiate it - then solve!

questions.question: Use implicit differentiation: if x^3 + y^3 = 6xy, find dy/dx.
questions.explanation: 3x^2 + 3y^2(dy/dx) = 6y + 6x(dy/dx). Collect dy/dx terms: dy/dx(3y^2 - 6x) = 6y - 3x^2. So dy/dx = (6y - 3x^2)/(3y^2 - 6x) = (2y - x^2)/(y^2 - 2x).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: product rule on 6xy, gather dy/dx terms, then divide - implicit victory!

questions.question: If x^2 + y^2 = 25, find the slope of the tangent line at (3, 4).
questions.explanation: dy/dx = -x/y from implicit differentiation. At (3, 4): -3/4.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: get dy/dx first, then feed in the point - plug and chug!

questions.question: If sin(x + y) = y, find dy/dx.
questions.explanation: cos(x+y)(1 + dy/dx) = dy/dx. So cos(x+y) = dy/dx(1 - cos(x+y)), giving dy/dx = cos(x+y)/(1 - cos(x+y)).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: chain rule inside implicit - the (1 + dy/dx) is the sneaky part!

questions.question: Maya inflates a spherical balloon so its radius increases at 2 cm/s. Find how fast the volume is increasing when r = 5 cm. (V = (4/3)pir^3)
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: related rates - differentiate with respect to TIME, then substitute!

questions.question: A 10-ft ladder slides down a wall. When the bottom is 6 ft from the wall, Alex measures it sliding out at 2 ft/s. Find how fast the top is sliding down.
questions.explanation: x^2 + y^2 = 100. When x = 6, y = 8. Differentiate: 2x(dx/dt) + 2y(dy/dt) = 0. So dy/dt = -(x/y)(dx/dt) = -(6/8)(2) = -1.5 ft/s.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: ladder problems - Pythagoras first, differentiate with time, watch the signs!

questions.question: Water pours into a conical tank (radius 4 m, height 8 m) at 3 m^3/min. Find how fast the water level is rising when h = 2 m.
questions.explanation: By similar triangles r/h = 4/8, so r = h/2. V = (1/3)πr^2h = (1/3)π(h/2)^2(h) = πh^3/12. Then dV/dt = (πh^2/4)(dh/dt). At h = 2: 3 = π(dh/dt), so dh/dt = 3/π m/min.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: cones need similar triangles first - kill the extra variable before differentiating!

questions.question: If f(x) = x^4 - 3x^2 + 1, find f''(x).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: second derivative - differentiate twice, no mercy!

questions.question: Find the critical numbers of f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2.
questions.explanation: f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x = 3x(x - 2). Set equal to 0: x = 0 or x = 2.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: critical numbers - where the derivative is zero or undefined!

questions.question: Find the x-value of the local maximum of f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2:
questions.explanation: f'(x) = 3x(x - 2). Sign chart: f' > 0 for x < 0, f' < 0 for 0 < x < 2. So f increases then decreases at x = 0: local max.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: first derivative test - plus to minus means a peak, a local max!

questions.question: Find the x-value of the local minimum of f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2:
questions.explanation: f' < 0 for 0 < x < 2 and f' > 0 for x > 2, so f decreases then increases at x = 2: local min.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: minus to plus means a valley - local minimum found!

questions.question: Find the absolute maximum of f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3 on [0, 5].
questions.explanation: f'(x) = 2x - 4 = 0 at x = 2. Check: f(0) = 3, f(2) = -1, f(5) = 8. Absolute max is 8 at x = 5.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: closed interval? Check critical points AND endpoints - no skipping!

questions.question: Find the absolute minimum of f(x) = x^3 - 3x on [-2, 2].
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: endpoints can tie with critical points - list every candidate value!

questions.question: If f''(x) > 0 on an interval, then f is:
questions.explanation: Positive second derivative means concave up (shaped like a cup).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: f-double-prime positive - the graph smiles like a happy dino cup!

questions.question: Find the inflection point(s) of f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 5.
questions.explanation: f''(x) = 6x - 12 = 0 at x = 2. f'' changes sign there (negative to positive), so x = 2 is an inflection point.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: inflection - where concavity flips, f-double-prime crosses zero!

questions.question: Identify the conditions under which the Mean Value Theorem applies to f on [a, b]:
questions.correctAnswer: Continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b)
questions.explanation: MVT requires continuity on the closed interval and differentiability on the open interval.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: MVT needs continuous on closed, differentiable on open - check both boxes!

questions.question: f(x) = x^2 on [0, 2]. Find c guaranteed by the Mean Value Theorem.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: MVT - secant slope equals tangent slope somewhere inside!

questions.question: If f'(x) > 0 for all x in (a, b), then f is:
questions.explanation: A positive first derivative means the function is increasing.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: f-prime positive - the graph climbs uphill!

questions.question: Farmer Diaz has 100 ft of fencing to enclose a rectangular pen against a barn (one side needs no fence). Find the maximum area.
questions.explanation: Let x = sides perpendicular to barn, y = side parallel. 2x + y = 100, so y = 100 - 2x. A = x(100 - 2x) = 100x - 2x^2. A' = 100 - 4x = 0 gives x = 25, y = 50. Max area = 1250.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: optimization - write area with one variable, differentiate, set to zero!

questions.question: Find the dimensions of the rectangle with perimeter 40 that has maximum area.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: fixed perimeter, max area - the answer is always a square!

questions.question: If f(x) = x^4, which statement about concavity is true?
distractors: Has an inflection point at x = 0
questions.explanation: f''(x) = 12x^2 >= 0 for all x, so f is concave up everywhere. At x = 0 concavity does not change, so no inflection point.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: x-to-the-fourth is a happy cup everywhere - no flip, no inflection!

questions.question: Use the second derivative test: f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 2 has what at x = 2?
questions.explanation: f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x, f''(x) = 6x - 6. At x = 2: f'(2) = 0 and f''(2) = 6 > 0, so local minimum.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: second derivative test - critical point plus positive f-double-prime means minimum!

questions.question: Find lim (x -> 0) (sin(3x)) / (5x).
questions.explanation: Rewrite as (3/5) * sin(3x)/(3x). Since sin(3x)/(3x) -> 1, the limit is 3/5.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: match the inside to the denominator, then the 3/5 pops out!

questions.question: Explain why f(x) = x^(2/3) has a critical number at x = 0:
questions.explanation: f'(x) = (2/3)x^(-1/3), which is undefined at x = 0. Critical numbers include points where the derivative is undefined.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: cusp at zero - derivative undefined means critical number!

questions.question: If the graph of f' changes from negative to positive at x = c, then f has a:
questions.explanation: By the First Derivative Test, f' changing from negative to positive means f decreases then increases: local minimum.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: read the f-prime sign chart like a story - down then up is a valley!

questions.question: Find the x-coordinate(s) where f(x) = x^4 - 4x^3 has horizontal tangent lines.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: horizontal tangent means derivative zero - factor and solve!

questions.question: Identify when Rolle's Theorem applies as a special case of the Mean Value Theorem:
questions.explanation: Rolle's Theorem adds the condition f(a) = f(b), which forces the MVT's secant slope to be 0, giving f'(c) = 0.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Rolle is MVT with equal endpoints - the tangent must go flat somewhere!

questions.question: Find the first step when differentiating f(x) = x^x using logarithmic differentiation:
questions.explanation: Take ln of both sides: ln(y) = ln(x^x) = x*ln(x). Then differentiate implicitly.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: variable in the exponent? Take logs first - logarithmic differentiation to the rescue!

questions.question: Find the indefinite integral: ∫ 3x^2 dx.
questions.explanation: Power rule for integrals: ∫ x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C. So ∫ 3x^2 dx = 3*(x^3/3) + C = x^3 + C.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: integration is differentiation in reverse - add one to the power, divide by the new power!

questions.question: Evaluate the definite integral: ∫(0 to 2) x^3 dx.
questions.explanation: Antiderivative: x^4/4. Evaluate: (2^4/4) - (0^4/4) = 16/4 - 0 = 4.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: definite integral - find antiderivative, plug top, minus plug bottom!

questions.question: Evaluate: ∫(1 to 3) (2x + 1) dx.
questions.explanation: Antiderivative: x^2 + x. At 3: 9 + 3 = 12. At 1: 1 + 1 = 2. Difference: 12 - 2 = 10.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: integrate term by term, then top minus bottom - steady dino steps!

questions.question: Find: ∫ e^(2x) dx.
questions.explanation: Use substitution u = 2x: ∫ e^u (du/2) = (1/2)e^u + C = (1/2)e^(2x) + C.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: chain rule in reverse - divide by the inner derivative!

questions.question: Find: ∫ x*e^(x^2) dx.
questions.explanation: Substitution u = x^2, du = 2x dx. ∫ x*e^(x^2) dx = (1/2)∫ e^u du = (1/2)e^u + C = (1/2)e^(x^2) + C.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: spot the inner function and its derivative hiding nearby - u-substitution!

questions.question: If F(x) = integral from a to x of f(t) dt with f continuous, find F'(x).
questions.explanation: FTC Part 1: the derivative of an accumulation function is the original integrand.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: derivative of an integral from a to x - the integral sign just vanishes!

questions.question: If F(x) = ∫(2 to x) t^3 dt, find F'(x).
questions.explanation: By FTC Part 1, F'(x) = x^3 (plug x into the integrand).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: lower limit is just a number - only the top x matters!

questions.question: If G(x) = ∫(x to 5) cos(t) dt, find G'(x).
questions.explanation: Flip the limits: G(x) = -∫(5 to x) cos(t) dt. By FTC: G'(x) = -cos(x). The variable on the bottom introduces a negative.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: x on the bottom? Flip it and slap on a negative sign!

questions.question: Evaluate: ∫(0 to π) sin(x) dx.
questions.explanation: Antiderivative: -cos(x). Evaluate: -cos(π) - (-cos(0)) = 1 + 1 = 2.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: sine from 0 to pi - the hump has area 2, picture it!

questions.question: Find: ∫ (1/x) dx.
questions.explanation: ∫ (1/x) dx = ln|x| + C. The absolute value handles negative x.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: one-over-x integrates to ln-absolute-x - the special power rule exception!

questions.question: Evaluate: ∫(1 to e) (1/x) dx.
questions.explanation: Antiderivative: ln|x|. ln(e) - ln(1) = 1 - 0 = 1.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: ln(e) is 1, ln(1) is 0 - the answer falls right out!

questions.question: If H(x) = ∫(1 to x^2) sqrt(t) dt, find H'(x).
questions.explanation: FTC with chain rule: H'(x) = sqrt(x^2) * d/dx[x^2] = sqrt(x^2) * 2x = 2x*sqrt(x^2).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: x-squared on top? FTC then chain rule - multiply by 2x!

questions.question: Find the area between y = x^2 and y = x from x = 0 to x = 1.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: area between curves - top minus bottom, then integrate!

questions.question: Find the area enclosed by y = 4 - x^2 and the x-axis.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: find where it hits zero first - those are your limits!

questions.question: Solve the differential equation dy/dx = 2x with y(0) = 5.
questions.explanation: Integrate: y = x^2 + C. Use y(0) = 5: 5 = 0 + C, so C = 5. Solution: y = x^2 + 5.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: separate, integrate, then use the point to find C - initial value victory!

questions.question: Solve dy/dx = y with y(0) = 3.
questions.explanation: dy/y = dx. Integrate: ln|y| = x + C, so y = Ae^x. y(0) = 3 gives A = 3. Solution: y = 3e^x.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: dy/dx = y means exponential - separate and watch e appear!

questions.question: Find the average value of f(x) = x^2 on [0, 3].
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: average value - one over width times the integral!

questions.question: Using a left Riemann sum with n = 2 subintervals, estimate ∫(0 to 2) x^2 dx.
questions.explanation: Width = 1. Left endpoints: x = 0, 1. Sum: (0^2)(1) + (1^2)(1) = 1.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: left sum uses left endpoints - multiply height by width, add them up!

questions.question: Using a right Riemann sum with n = 2 subintervals, estimate ∫(0 to 2) x^2 dx.
questions.explanation: Width = 1. Right endpoints: x = 1, 2. Sum: (1^2)(1) + (2^2)(1) = 1 + 4 = 5.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: right sum uses right endpoints - for increasing functions it overestimates!

questions.question: If f is continuous and ∫(0 to 4) f(x) dx = 10 and ∫(0 to 4) g(x) dx = 3, find ∫(0 to 4) [2f(x) - g(x)] dx.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: integrals are linear - constants pull out, sums split apart!
